strengths: Clear and well-motivated empirical observation ('shift-readapt-overfit' progression) that explains why SFT-then-RL can underperform pure RL, providing useful insight into training dynamics when off-policy expert data diverges strongly from the model's established policy.
The proposed dual-control mechanism (global coefficient µ + token-wise weighting function ϕ) is simple, interpretable, and easy to implement within a standard GRPO-style pipeline.

The parabolic weighting function ϕ(pt)=pt(1-pt) is intuitively motivated by an uncertainty/entropy argument and empirically shown to mitigate both entropy collapse (from plain IS) and entropy blow-up (from unweighted mixing).

Reasonably comprehensive experiments spanning two different tasks (math reasoning and tool-use) and two different base models, with a good set of baselines (SFT-only, RL-only, SFT+RL, SASR, LUFFY) plus multiple ablations (fixed vs. decayed µ, with/without ϕ, warmup-decay schedule) and qualitative case studies showing behavioral differences.

Useful supplementary analysis distinguishing off-policy effects on base vs. instruction-tuned models, which clarifies the paper's specific and underexplored setting (fine-tuning an already well-aligned instruct model with off-policy experts).
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: reweighting SFT loss and dynamically scheduling its coefficient during RL builds directly on ideas already explored in cited works (LUFFY, SRFT, SASR, In-RIL, iw-SFT/DFT); the core technical contribution (a symmetric p(1-p) token weight and a linear/exponential µ decay) is fairly simple and not deeply justified theoretically beyond an informal entropy/uncertainty argument.

Comparisons to the most relevant recent baseline, SRFT, are only discussed qualitatively in related work but not included in the main experimental comparison, weakening the empirical positioning against the closest competing method.
The LUFFY baseline is trained with less data (20k vs. its original 45k) due to the authors' setup, which could unfairly disadvantage this baseline and makes the comparison less controlled.

Gains over strong baselines are sometimes small or mixed (e.g., CHORD-φ underperforms CHORD-µ on AIME25; CHORD-µ underperforms SFT-best+RL on MMLU-Pro), and it is unclear whether the differences are statistically significant given the relatively small benchmark sizes (e.g., AIME24/25 have only 30 problems) and apparent single-seed reporting for most tables.

Experiments are limited to two backbone models (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and LLaMA3.2-3B-Instruct) and two task domains; scalability to larger models or more diverse tasks (e.g., open-ended generation, code) is untested, limiting evidence for general applicability.

The token-wise weighting function is only compared against plain IS and no-IS ablations; no comparison to alternative principled weighting schemes (e.g., entropy-based, confidence-based, or learned weighting) is provided to justify the specific choice of p(1-p) beyond its intuitive appeal.

Hyperparameter sensitivity (e.g., decay rate/shape for µ, fixed µ value used with ϕ) is only partially explored, and the practical recipe for selecting these values across new tasks is not clearly specified, which may hinder reproducibility.

The tool-use experiments use a very small SFT set (500 examples) and only single-turn ToolAce instances, raising questions about how well the findings generalize to more complex, multi-turn or larger-scale tool-use settings.

strengths: Provides a clear and interesting empirical analysis (the 'shift-readapt-overfit' progression) that motivates the proposed method and gives insight into why SFT-then-RL pipelines can underperform pure RL when fine-tuning already-aligned instruct models.

The dual-control mechanism (global coefficient µ for macro-level scheduling and token-wise weighting φ(p)=p(1-p) for micro-level stability) is intuitive, computationally cheap (element-wise multiplication on existing forward-pass probabilities), and well motivated by the entropy-collapse/entropy-explosion trade-off shown in Figure 5.

Extensive experimentation: two distinct task families (math reasoning and tool use), multiple base models (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, LLaMA3.2-3B-Instruct), and a large appendix with many additional studies (adaptive µ, alternative φ variants including entropy-based/focal loss/IS-clip, different expert data sources, non-verifiable domains, weaker policy models, MoE architecture, base vs instruct model comparisons) that substantially strengthen the empirical case.

Comparisons against a comprehensive and relevant set of baselines (SFT-only, SFT+RL, LUFFY, SASR, and in the appendix SRFT), with discussion of why CHORD is particularly suited to the instruct-model fine-tuning setting as opposed to the 'zero-RL' setting most prior work targets.

Qualitative case studies (Appendix E) provide convincing, human-readable evidence that CHORD-φ produces a hybrid reasoning style that blends conciseness with selective adoption of expert verification patterns, supporting the quantitative claims.
Reasonably thorough experimental setup documentation (Appendix A) with hyperparameters, prompts, and reward functions, aiding reproducibility, along with a promise to release code.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is somewhat incremental: dynamically weighting SFT/RL losses and token-wise reweighting of off-policy signals have been explored in related works (SRFT, LUFFY, SASR, UFT, BREAD); the paper's main differentiator (targeting already-instruction-tuned models rather than base models) is a useful but relatively narrow framing rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea.

The φ(p)=p(1-p) weighting function, while empirically effective, is a fairly ad hoc heuristic; the 'information-theoretic' justification is thin, and the paper itself acknowledges in Section 4.3 that it is 'unlikely a single universally optimal design exists,' which somewhat undercuts the principledness of the contribution.

Baseline comparisons are not always matched in data budget (e.g., LUFFY is evaluated with fewer training samples than its original paper, and SFT data sizes vary substantially across methods—500 vs 5k for tool-use), which could bias some comparisons in CHORD's favor or make them harder to interpret.

Despite claims that φ(·) reduces sensitivity to µ, the overall framework still involves multiple interacting hyperparameters (µ initial value, decay schedule/steps, fixed µ choice, φ formulation) that require tuning per task, somewhat undermining the 'simplification' claim.

Reported results lack clear variance/statistical significance measures for most tables (aside from avg@32/avg@8 on a few reasoning benchmarks), making it harder to assess whether the (often modest, e.g., +0.1–2.4 point) improvements over strong baselines like GRPO/SFT-best+RL are robust.

The theoretical understanding of why the shift-readapt-overfit dynamic occurs, and why the specific token-wise weighting is optimal, remains largely empirical/qualitative rather than formally grounded, which the authors themselves note as a limitation for future work.
